reverse_outline.summary: Three takeaways: physical systems own their facts, promises are computed from inputs, one writer per fact and one source per view
Physical fulfilment work after checkout decides whether delivery happens on time
Timeline of Eva's jacket order: late delivery and size exchange
Kestrel & Pine introduced with its fulfilment volumes and channels
Waypoint's three rules: single writer per fact, promises computed from its events, all views read one order record
Roadmap of the part following Eva's parcel out and back
Warehouse chapter: order-management/warehouse contract and the Black Friday backlog incident
Shipping chapter: carrier integration and delivery dates computed from real inputs, not a fixed rule
Stores chapter: till as a data source and the Utrecht store-stock incident
Returns chapter: separate states and owners for return steps, shown by the double refunds
Customer service chapter: aligning messages, status page and support view after the three-status order
Closing: failures came from promises made without inputs; start with the warehouse chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All eleven summaries match their aligned spec paragraphs' controlling ideas in the same order; the callout is the KEY POINTS evidence of p04. Small drift only: the p08 summary omits the alternative routes and the p09 summary omits that refund and restock wait for inspection.
The outliner marked no unit as carrying two ideas; the three-bullet KEY POINTS callout is the shape the house style requires.

¶1-¶3 set up the gap and scenario the thesis answers, ¶4 states P4-1, P4-3/P4-4 and P4-5 as three rules, and each chapter paragraph introduces the chapter carrying its declared claims; P4-2's keyed accept-or-reject instruction is only named (as 'the work instruction and response'), as the spec allows.

Each case is followed or framed by what it shows ('shows why a warehouse can have spare picking capacity...', 'show why each action needs its own state...', 'drew eleven tickets because...'); the volumes are framed as 'makes such promises at scale'. The Store Stock Mirage is the thinnest: what it shows (a promise read from a copy, not the till) is left implicit, but the surrounding sentences draw the data lesson.

p02 'Eva's jacket order shows this sequence' (example), p03 'Eva bought from' (elaboration), p04 'At each step ... draws three rules from this' (cause_effect), p05 'The chapters follow Eva's parcel' (sequence; also the section's end_of_previous elaboration), p07 'Then', p08 'Off Eva's route' (contrast), p09 'On the way back', p10 'Last', and the closing's summary sentence all express their declared relationships. p10's 'Last' gives the sequence but not its declared carry-over (the events of the earlier chapters), which flow-A noted the reader must infer.

Both readers found the page easy to follow and describe the declared organisation (problem, example, company, rules, roadmap, then chapters in the order of Eva's parcel out and back, stores as a side trip); no section's position is unclear. Undefined 'order record', 'Waypoint' and the incident names, flagged by both, are in audience.already_knows (Parts I to III) and are not counted as lost-thread points; failures follow as separate results.

results.quote: Last, [[customer-service-and-notifications]] aligns **messages, the status page and the support view**.
results.finding: Both readers re-read Figure 3's caption because it lists the Three-Status Order before the Double Refund while the chapters put returns before service (flow-A item 12: 'The incident order here (Three-Status before Double Refund) differs from the chapter order'). The order is fixed by the spec's Figure 3 evidence.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 5: 'The chapters present the Double Refund before the Three-Status Order, but the caption swaps them.'

results.quote: Last, [[customer-service-and-notifications]] aligns **messages, the status page and the support view**.
results.finding: Both readers could not reconcile Figure 3's four promises with five chapters, nor its pairing of 'delivered tomorrow' with the Queue That Waited (the text tied that promise to Eva and shipping) and 'your order was delivered' with the Three-Status Order (described as a two-parcel problem). The count and pairing are declared in the spec.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 5: 'The caption pairs "delivered tomorrow" with the Queue That Waited ... There are five chapters and four promises'

results.quote: None of these cases needed faster work
results.finding: Both readers met 'faster work' as a new contrast nothing earlier sets up (flow-A item 13: 'None needed faster work is a new claim'). The spec's synthesis sets the cases against faster work, but no earlier unit is assigned to state the disputed view, so the prose cannot prepare it within the spec.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 10: '"Faster work" is a new contrast that nothing earlier sets up.'

results.quote: The Three-Status Order drew eleven tickets because no system could say the order ships in two parcels.
results.finding: Both readers could not connect the name 'Three-Status Order' to the given cause (two parcels) and had to guess that three screens showed three statuses (flow-A item 11). A few words saying three systems showed three different statuses would close it.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B item 19: 'The Three-Status Order: the name is never explained ... The text gives only the two-parcel cause.'

results.quote: The system that knows a fact is its only writer: for returns, the warehouse's returns bench, where items are inspected.
results.finding: flow-B paused because the only example of the one-writer rule jumps to returns while the text had been walking the parcel outward. The returns-bench example is the spec's choice for p04 (single reader, minor).

results.quote: Returns and store collections depend on the same work.
results.finding: flow-A re-read to separate 'store collections' (customers collecting in store) from 'the carrier's collection' in the sentence before (single reader, minor).

results.quote: The Queue That Waited, a four-hour Black Friday backlog, shows why a warehouse can have spare picking capacity while customers wait for orders that never reached it.
results.finding: flow-B re-read to reconcile a backlog with spare capacity; that the queue sat before the warehouse, not in it, is implied but not stated (single reader, minor).

results.quote: Store pickup and counter exchange provide alternative routes.
results.finding: flow-B could not tell what these are alternative routes for (single reader, minor).

results.quote: Eva's size exchange and January 2027's 212 double refunds (the Double Refund) show why each action needs its own state and authorized owner.
results.finding: flow-A found this sentence dense: four steps, two cases and two requirements in one sentence (single reader, minor).

The three does_not_know terms are handled as the spec allows: the returns bench is glossed ('where items are inspected'), the pick wave is glossed in ¶2 of the chapters ('the 21:00 picking batch') and the KEY POINTS uses the plain 'picking batch', and 'the work instruction and response' is only named. Terms both readers flagged (order record, order management, Waypoint, writer, keyed, incident names) are in already_knows from Parts I to III.
The introduction opens on a concrete puzzling scenario (seconds at checkout against a day's slip) and a dated worked order; no placeholder, restated question, definition or book-report opening.

The closing applies the KEY POINTS diagnosis to every case including the opening's late delivery and gives a course of action; it is not a bare rephrased thesis, grab bag or 'in conclusion'. Its 'faster work' contrast is recorded under flow_is_followable.

'each promise, like the opening's late delivery, was made without its inputs' synthesizes the cases, and 'Begin with [[warehouse-and-fulfillment]], where Eva's paid order reaches Duiven' gives the so-what and takeaway.
'like the opening's late delivery' calls back to ¶1's day-slip and Eva's day-late delivery in ¶2, naming it as one more promise made without its inputs.
The intro reader predicted the roadmap exactly: warehouse, carrier and delivery date, a side trip to the stores, return and refund, and the status the customer sees, in that order.

The cold reader named the five chapter subjects in reading order; the finer elements of `expected` (instruction and response, the till as a source, the separate return steps with owners, the shared status) are stated in bold in each chapter paragraph, so a reader of the whole page finds them.

The reader explained that a fixed storefront rule ignored that the 21:14 order missed Duiven's 21:00 picking batch, and that the promise should be computed from the picking batch, backlog, collection schedules, location and carrier performance, matching `expected`.
